title: Air Navigation Systems
description: Key concepts from AIM Chapter 1 covering navigation aids, GPS, WAAS, ILS, and Performance-Based Navigation

cards.back:
• Frequency: 190-535 kHz (low/medium frequency)
• Provides bearing information to 'home' on station
• Uses ADF (Automatic Direction Finder) receiver
• No flag warning for erroneous bearings - monitor ID continuously
• Vulnerable to lightning, precipitation static, and nighttime interference

• Frequency: 108.0-117.95 MHz (VHF band)
• Subject to line-of-sight restrictions
• Range varies with altitude
• Accuracy: ±1 degree
• 'W' suffix (VORW) = Without voice capability
• Identify by Morse code or 'VOR' voice announcement

• VOT frequency found in Chart Supplement
• With CDI centered: OBS should show 0° FROM or 180° TO
• Maximum error for IFR: ±4° (VOT check)
• RMI will show 180° on any OBS setting
• Check required within 30 days for IFR flight
• Other methods: airborne checkpoint, ground checkpoint, dual VOR check

• TACAN: Military/naval navigation system
• Operates in UHF band (pulse system)
• Provides both azimuth AND distance
• VOR provides azimuth only (needs separate DME for distance)
• TACAN developed for shipboard/unusual siting conditions
• Requires specific TACAN airborne equipment

• Combined VOR + TACAN at one site
• Provides THREE services:
 1. VOR azimuth (civilian)
 2. TACAN azimuth (military)
 3. TACAN distance/DME (both)
• Frequencies are 'paired' for simplified operation
• Both signals have interlocked identification

• Frequency: 960-1215 MHz (UHF)
• Provides SLANT RANGE distance (not horizontal)
• Accuracy: ½ mile or 3% (whichever greater)
• Range: up to 199 NM at line-of-sight altitude
• Aircraft interrogates; ground transponder replies
• Paired with VOR/VORTAC frequencies for auto-selection

• DME shows slant range (straight-line distance to station)
• Slant range > horizontal distance (especially close to station at altitude)
• Example: Directly over station at 6,000 ft AGL, DME shows 1 NM
• Error decreases with distance from station
• Plan approaches accounting for this difference

THREE functional parts:
1. GUIDANCE: Localizer (lateral) + Glideslope (vertical)
2. RANGE: Marker beacons + DME
3. VISUAL: Approach lights, touchdown/centerline lights, runway lights

Basic components: Localizer, Glideslope, Outer Marker (OM), Inner Marker (IM for Cat II/III)

• Frequency: 108.10-111.95 MHz
• Transmitter at far end of runway
• Course width: 700 feet at threshold
• Provides runway centerline alignment
• Front course = approach course
• Back course = opposite direction (reverse sensing without special equipment)

OUTER MARKER (OM):
• Blue light, continuous dashes
• Marks FAF/glideslope intercept

MIDDLE MARKER (MM):
• Amber light, alternating dots/dashes
• ~3,500 ft from runway, ~200 ft above threshold

INNER MARKER (IM):
• White light, continuous dots
• Cat II/III decision point

• Back course is opposite direction from front course
• WITHOUT reverse sensing: Steer OPPOSITE needle deflection
• Needle right = fly left, needle left = fly right
• With reverse sensing equipment: Normal needle interpretation
• Glideslope NOT valid on back course
• Published as LOC BC approach

• Similar to localizer but LESS precise
• Frequency: 108.10-111.95 MHz
• NO glideslope information
• Course width: 6° or 12° (vs ~5° for localizer)
• Course may NOT be aligned with runway
• Usable off-course indications: 35° either side
• Approach leads to SDF antenna, not runway centerline

During maintenance:
• Coded identification REMOVED (warning that facility unreliable)
• VHF ranges may transmit T-E-S-T code (- • ••• -)
• DO NOT fly procedure NOTAMed out of service
• Even if signal present, facility may be unreliable
• Always check NOTAMs before flight

IRU (Inertial Reference Unit):
• Gyros + accelerometers
• Provides attitude, position, velocity
• Position degrades over time (drift)

INS (Inertial Navigation System):
• IRU + navigation computer
• Can navigate via waypoints

AHRS (Attitude Heading Reference System):
• Provides attitude only, no position

• Materials under taxiways/ramps create magnetic fields
• Can affect slaved compass flux detector
• Causes erroneous heading alignment
• May NOT self-correct
• Check heading alignment before takeoff
• Follow manufacturer procedures to correct

• 24-satellite constellation
• Minimum 4 satellites for 3D position
• 5 satellites always visible worldwide (design goal)
• Uses WGS-84 coordinate system
• DoD operates satellite constellation
• Status broadcast in data message and via NOTAMs

• GPS receiver self-checks integrity
• Without RAIM: No assurance of position accuracy
• Requires: 5 satellites OR 4 satellites + baro-aiding
• Provides immediate pilot feedback
• FDE (Fault Detection and Exclusion): Can exclude bad satellite
• Critical for IFR GPS operations

• Delays up to 2 hours before erroneous satellite detected by control segment
• RAIM provides real-time detection
• Must have current database
• Check RAIM availability before IFR approach
• Not all GPS receivers approved for all operations
• TSO certification determines capabilities

• Improves GPS accuracy, integrity, availability
• Broadcasts on GPS L1 frequency (1575.42 MHz)
• Uses Wide-area Reference Stations (WRS)
• Corrections via geostationary satellites (GEO)
• Enables LPV approaches (vertical guidance)
• Similar systems: EGNOS (Europe), GAGAN (India)

• 38 Wide-area Reference Stations (WRS)
• 3 Wide-area Master Stations (WMS)
• 3 GEO satellite links
• 6 Ground Earth Stations (GES)
• 2 Operational Control Centers
• GEO also provides additional ranging signal

GBAS (Ground Based Augmentation System):
• Local differential GPS augmentation
• 4+ reference stations at airport
• VHF Data Broadcast (VDB) uplink

GLS (GBAS Landing System):
• Precision approach like ILS
• 3D lateral and vertical guidance
• Single ground station supports multiple runways

Performance-Based Navigation:
• RNAV: Area navigation (general term)
• Two NavSpec categories:
 1. RNAV x: Specified accuracy
 2. RNP x: RNAV + onboard monitoring/alerting
• Number = lateral accuracy in NM (95% of time)
• Example: RNP 1 = 1 NM accuracy, 95% of flight time

RNAV:
• Area navigation capability
• Specified accuracy requirement
• No onboard performance monitoring required

RNP (Required Navigation Performance):
• RNAV + OBPMA (Onboard Performance Monitoring and Alerting)
• Aircraft verifies it meets requirements
• Allows reduced ATC intervention
• Enables tighter separation

• NavSpecs are DIFFERENT, not better/worse
• RNP 1 eligibility does NOT mean RNAV 1 eligibility
• Each eligibility listed separately in AFM
• Database holds only procedures aircraft is eligible for
• If procedure not in database, aircraft may be ineligible
• Verify procedure data after loading

Suitable RNAV can substitute when:
• NAVAID is out of service (per NOTAM)
• Aircraft not equipped with ADF or DME
• ADF or DME is inoperative

Example: Hold over out-of-service NDB using GPS
• Must meet AC 90-108 requirements
• May need to advise ATC of intent

Suitable RNAV can be used when:
• NAVAID is operational
• Aircraft has working compatible equipment
• Flying procedure without monitoring ground navaid

Example: Fly VOR procedure using GPS without monitoring VOR
• Per AC 90-108 requirements
• Database must be current

Impacts include:
• Loss of GPS navigation
• Loss of hybrid GPS/inertial navigation
• Degraded PBN capability
• Unreliable TAWS triggering
• Erroneous ADS-B outputs
• Unexpected autotuning effects
• Erroneous FMS calculations
• ATM infrastructure failures

• Intentional false GPS signals
• Can cause unflagged position errors
• RAIM only partially effective against spoofing
• Pilot may NOT be aware of errors
• ATC may be only means to detect
• GPS re-radiators (maintenance) Can cause unintentional spoofing

When experiencing GPS problems:
1. Transition to another navigation source
2. Request amended clearances from ATC
3. Report anomaly as soon as practical

Report should include:
• Date/time and NAVAID ID
• Location (lat/long or bearing/distance)
• Heading, altitude, aircraft type/callsign

• FAA removing selected VORs as GPS/RNAV adopted
• MON: Subset of VORs retained as backup
• Ensures navigation if GPS unavailable
• GPS is primary navigation for PBN
• MON provides contingency capability
• Check Chart Supplement for MON status

• NDB: 190-535 kHz (LF/MF)
• VOR: 108.0-117.95 MHz (VHF)
• Localizer: 108.10-111.95 MHz (VHF)
• Glideslope: 329-335 MHz (UHF)
• DME/TACAN: 960-1215 MHz (UHF)
• GPS L1: 1575.42 MHz

• NDB co-located with ILS marker
• LOM: Locator Outer Marker
• LMM: Locator Middle Marker
• Two-letter identifier
• Provides NDB guidance to marker location
• Helps pilots find ILS course

CAT I:
• DH: 200 ft
• Visibility: 1800 RVR or ½ mile

CAT II:
• DH: 100-200 ft
• Visibility: 1200 RVR
• Requires special equipment/training

CAT III:
• DH: <100 ft or none
• Visibility: 700 RVR down to 0
• Autoland capable aircraft

• Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance
• WAAS-enabled GPS approach
• Precision-like vertical guidance
• Decision Altitude (DA) like ILS
• Minimums can be as low as 200 ft
• NOT technically a precision approach (APV)
• Requires WAAS receiver

• Line-of-sight only (terrain/altitude dependent)
• Propeller RPM can cause ±6° CDI fluctuation
• Mountain terrain can cause needle oscillation
• Some receivers more susceptible to irregularities
• No 'flag' for some types of errors
• Annual calibration recommended
